stories.headline: India’s largest earthquake-isolated hospital block coming up at LD Hospital
stories.title: India’s largest earthquake-isolated hospital block coming up at LD Hospital
stories.summary: Srinagar, Nov 24: This building is designed to move with the earthquakes. In one of India's most earthquake-vulnerable regions, Kashmir, a major engineering initiative is shaping country's largest purpose-designed hospital structure. The six-storey structure at Lal Ded Hospital Srinagar incorporates advanced seismic base-isolation technology, and is nearing completion soon. The World Bank funded extension block at the premier maternity hospital has been conceived around earthquake-isolation technology from its design stage. Most such structures have the system introduced as a subsequent structural retrofit. The building incorporates 43 friction pendulum isolators. These are designed to reduce the transfer of seismic forces from the ground to the structure during an earthquake. The LD Hospital project is the largest among three such base-isolation projects in India. The project is among the India’s significant applications of the technology in hospital infrastructure. This project is being executed under the Jhelum and Tawi Flood Recovery Project (JTFRP). Medical Superintendent Lal Ded Hospital, Dr Muzaffar Jan said the project is an engineering marvel, not just for J&K, but for the entire country. The base-isolation system is the key and differentiating feature of the building's structural design. In conventional construction the foundation is rigidly connected to the superstructure. In base isolation system, specially engineered bearings allow controlled movement between the building and the ground during seismic activity. The friction pendulum system uses sliding bearings with curved surfaces to help dissipate earthquake energy. It also limits the forces transmitted to the structure. The 43 isolators are intended to provide an additional layer of protection to a critical healthcare facility. Dr Jan said the building can bear a quake upto the intensity of 8 Richter scale. The design and engineering components have undergone technical vetting by premier institutions. This project demonstrates a significant application of advanced seismic engineering in public healthcare infrastructure. The MS, Dr Jan, said the original allotted cost of Rs 118.22 crore has been revised to Rs 127.75 crore now. The G+5 structure with an attic has a total built-up area of 11,640 square metres. Its specialised bed strength has been revised from 108 to 117. It will have 65 adult beds and 52 infant beds. The block will house specialties of gynae-oncology and assisted fertility and will house specialised healthcare infrastructure. This includes modular operation theatres, intensive care units, high-dependency units, neonatal intensive care facilities, Labour, Delivery and Recovery suites, IVF laboratories and advanced foetal intervention facilities. Component-wise progress shows civil works at 75 percent. On the same lines, electrical works have been completed 78 percent while mechanical works are at 71 percent. Sixty-two percent medical equipment has been procured. The agreement for execution of the project was signed on August 1, 2025. The original completion deadline was December 31, 2026, and now the revised completion date has been fixed as February 28, 2027. The project is part of the reconstruction and augmentation of critical hospital infrastructure under the World Bank-funded JTFRP. The proposal was approved in 2017, but the project subsequently faced prolonged delays.

stories.headline: Before polls, UP chief election officer flags slow voter enrolment in Noida, Gr Noida
stories.title: Before polls, UP chief election officer flags slow voter enrolment in Noida, Gr Noida
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: At a late-evening meeting attended by Uttar Pradesh Chief Election Officer Navdeep Rinwa and other election officials in Noida on Monday, senior officers flagged the poor performance of the Gautam Buddha Nagar district in the last seven days in terms of voter enrolment, The Indian Express has learnt.
According to a senior state election officer, while Gautam Buddha Nagar, where Noida and Greater Noida are located, lags behind, Ghaziabad, the neighbouring district, performed better.
This comes as the state is expected to hold Assembly elections next year in February.
The UP draft electoral roll was published on November 17 as part of a Special Summary Revision exercise, registering an addition of 18.84 lakh voters to the list.
Gautam Buddha Nagar district logged a rise of 22,346 voters, compared with the final roll published following a Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls, on April 10 this year.
In Ghaziabad, 61,235 new voters registered.
The seven days that followed were closely watched across districts, when claims and objections were filed, officers said.
The performance was assessed based on two indicators — the number of Form 6 received per polling station in the district and inclusion of potential voters in the electoral roll.

In the last seven days, an officer said, about 20 forms were filled at each of Ghaziabad’s 3,000-odd polling booths, while at Gautam Buddha Nagar, an average of six forms were filled at each of its 1,926 polling stations.
In this parameter, out of the total 75 districts in the state, while Ghaziabad ranked first, Gautam Buddha Nagar stood at 32.
Explaining the second parameter, the officer said, the total number of registered electors on the rolls are subtracted from the population projection till 2036.
“We then estimate the number of eligible population still out of the rolls.

stories.headline: Govt to revive Kashmir’s only olive cultivation belt
stories.title: Govt to revive Kashmir’s only olive cultivation belt
stories.summary: Srinagar, Nov 24: The government has constituted a committee to revive Kashmir’s only established olive cultivation belt in the Salamabad area of Uri in north Kashmir’s Baramulla district, which is facing a gradual decline due to the prolonged absence of a reliable irrigation facility. The 29-kanal olive plantation, located near the Line of Control (LoC), has been struggling for years as the lack of adequate water supply has affected the growth and productivity of trees, raising concerns over the future of the region’s unique olive-growing legacy. Joint Director Horticulture Kashmir Javaid Bhat told Rising Kashmir that the department has constituted a committee comprising four to five officials to explore measures for reviving the plantation. “I have constituted a committee comprising four to five officials, who are working on ways to revive the olive belt,” he said. Bhat said the department was also planning to introduce new rows of olive trees, experiment with other crops and explore high-density plantations to improve productivity. He said efforts were being made to identify a sustainable source of irrigation, including the possibility of lifting water from the Jhelum River to irrigate the orchard. Another horticulture department official said the department had approached the Irrigation Department in Uri to explore the possibility of lifting water from the river, but the proposal had not received a positive response. “We are now planning to approach NHPC authorities, which have a reservoir near the olive plantation, and request their intervention to help restore the irrigation facility,” the official said. He said the prolonged absence of irrigation had considerably affected the health and productivity of olive trees. “The growth and productivity of olive trees have reduced considerably. Without a dependable source of irrigation, sustaining the plantation has become increasingly difficult,” the official said. The plantation was established in 1987 under an Indo-Italian collaboration and initially had access to a natural stream. Water from the stream was collected in a tank and subsequently used to irrigate the orchard. However, the 2005 earthquake damaged the water supply system, leaving the plantation without a reliable irrigation source. Since then, rainfall has remained the primary source of moisture for the trees, contributing to a gradual decline in their growth and yield. The department has also explored alternative ways to restore irrigation. In 2024, the Irrigation Department inspected the site to assess the feasibility of developing a groundwater source. “They had proposed digging a borewell, but the plan could not be implemented because of the area’s higher elevation, which makes groundwater extraction technically difficult,” the official said. The irrigation crisis has affected not only olive production but also the broader objective of promoting olive oil extraction in the region. Olive cultivation in Kashmir remains largely confined to the Uri region, where relatively warmer climatic conditions and suitable soil have provided a favourable environment for the Mediterranean crop. The Salamabad plantation was established after soil studies conducted by a British team identified the area as suitable for olive cultivation. The project was subsequently taken up in 1987 under an Indo-Italian collaboration as an important initiative to diversify horticulture in the region. Local residents and growers have expressed concern over the gradual deterioration of the plantation, saying immediate government intervention is necessary to prevent Kashmir's only established olive-growing belt from further decline.

stories.headline: SC to hear bail pleas of Umar Khalid, Sharjeel Imam in 2020 Delhi riots conspiracy case
stories.title: SC to hear bail pleas of Umar Khalid, Sharjeel Imam in 2020 Delhi riots conspiracy case
stories.summary: A bench of Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V. Mohana is slated to take up both matters

article_sentences: New Delhi: The Supreme Court is slated to hear on Wednesday the separate petitions filed by jailed student activists Umar Khalid and Sharjeel Imam challenging the Delhi High Court's judgment rejecting their fresh bail pleas in the 2020 northeast Delhi riots "larger conspiracy" case.

A bench of Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V. Mohana is slated to take up both matters, according to the cause list published on the official website of the apex court.
Khalid's petition has been registered as SLP (Crl.) No. 22342/2026, while Imam's plea has been registered as SLP (Crl.) No. 22241/2026.

The petitions challenge a common judgment delivered on September 30 by a Division Bench of the Delhi High Court comprising Justices Prathiba M. Singh and Dinesh Bhatt, which had rejected their appeals against the trial court's July 4, 2026, orders refusing them regular bail.
The Delhi High Court ruled that it could not alter the conditions set by the Supreme Court when it rejected the earlier bail pleas of Umar Khalid and Sharjeel Imam in January 2026.
In its January 5 order, the Supreme Court had denied them bail but allowed them to reapply after the examination of key prosecution witnesses or a year after the judgment, whichever occurred first.

In June 2026, Khalid and Imam again approached the trial court, citing new developments such as the Supreme Court’s remarks on prolonged incarceration and trial delays in a different UAPA case, interim bail granted to co-accused Tasleem Ahmed and Khalid Saifi, and the additional time spent in jail.
After the trial court dismissed their bail pleas, the activists approached the Delhi High Court.
They argued that the trial was unlikely to conclude soon and that their continued detention without substantial progress justified reconsideration of their bail.
However, the High Court maintained that it could not go beyond the liberty specifically granted by the Supreme Court.
It noted that the Supreme Court had clearly distinguished the roles of Khalid and Imam from those of co-accused who had secured bail.

The High Court further held that the cases of Tasleem Ahmed and Khalid Saifi were not comparable to those of Khalid and Imam, whose alleged roles had been described as "masterminds" and "core conspirators" in the Supreme Court’s earlier ruling.

stories.headline: Warwan glacial lake threatens downstream villages
stories.title: Warwan glacial lake threatens downstream villages
stories.summary: Srinagar, Nov 22: An expanding glacial lake in Kishtwar's remote Warwan Valley poses a potential flood threat to downstream villages in Warwan and Marwah, while raising concerns over hydropower infrastructure farther downstream in Kishtwar district, according to a new scientific study. A worst-case simulation shows that an avalanche striking Lake-B in the Fariabaad Nalla catchment could release 97.5 percent of its stored water, generating a peak discharge of 2214 cubic metres per second immediately below the lake. The resulting flood could travel about 65 km and reach a point just upstream of Qaderna village in Marwah Valley within six hours. The study identifies nine bridges, 40 buildings and several road networks within the potential inundation zone, particularly along the Marusudar River, a major tributary of the Chenab, near Yurod and Qaderna. It also examines the potential exposure of Kishtwar's Bursar (800 MW) and Pakal Dul (1000 MW) hydropower projects, located around 90 km downstream of the glacier complex. However, both projects lie beyond the study's 85-km flood-routing domain, and the researchers did not simulate flood arrival at either site or quantify possible damage. Published on November 4, 2026, in the journal Natural Hazards and Earth System Sciences, the study reconstructs an avalanche-triggered glacial lake outburst flood (GLOF) in September 2020 and assesses the potential consequences of a future outburst from another lake in the Warwan sub-basin. Worst-case scenario could release 97.5% of lake water The researchers modelled three scenarios involving avalanches of different magnitudes striking Lake-B. In the worst-case scenario, a 25-million-cubic-metre rock-ice avalanche entering the lake could generate a peak water discharge of 2214 cubic metres per second. The avalanche debris could add another 1316 cubic metres per second to the flow immediately below the lake. The simulation estimates that 97.5 percent of the lake's stored water could be released. A moderate avalanche could drain 91 percent, while a lower-magnitude event could release about 85.7 percent. Further downstream, peak discharge could reach 621 cubic metres per second at a section 49 km from the lake before declining to 535 cubic metres per second near Qaderna, approximately 65 km downstream, by the sixth hour. Maximum flow depths at these two locations were estimated at 2.8 metres and 2 metres. At locations with infrastructure, the model indicated possible flow depths of two to four metres and velocities of four to six metres per second. The researchers cautioned that the simulations represent potential scenarios, not a prediction that an outburst will occur. 2020 avalanche triggered GLOF from Lake-A The study reconstructed an earlier event in September 2020, when a rock-ice avalanche struck Lake-A, displacing its stored water and sediment and triggering a GLOF followed by a downstream debris flow. The avalanche originated from the accumulation zone of glacier GL-A at an altitude of about 4890 metres. It travelled 2355 metres and covered a mapped area of around 0.78 sq km. Satellite imagery taken before and after the event showed that the lake's moraine was breached, its outlet channel widened and debris was deposited downstream. According to the researchers, sediment carried by meltwater streams from adjoining glaciers GL-D and GL-E had gradually accumulated in Lake-A, dividing it into two basins. The avalanche impact displaced the stored water and sediment, sending the material downstream. The outburst did not trigger a second GLOF from Lake-B, located immediately downstream. A smaller proglacial lake later re-formed at the terminus of GL-A. The study also documented two other major avalanche events in the glacier complex. An avalanche in September 2005 originated from the headwall of glacier GL-B and travelled about 2620 metres but stopped before reaching its lake. In March 2020, a rock-ice avalanche from glacier GL-F travelled around 2,470 metres, affecting an area of about 1.24 sq km, but did not reach a glacial lake. Lake-B expands 308% in 25 years Satellite imagery showed that Lake-B expanded from about 0.07 sq km in 1999 to 0.306 sq km in 2024, an increase of approximately 308 percent. The researchers attributed the expansion to glacier retreat, meltwater inflow and repeated ice-calving events. A reconstruction of the glacier bed placed the lake's potential maximum volume at 7.7 million cubic metres, while a separate volume-area scaling method produced a comparable estimate of 7.4 million cubic metres. The wider Fariabaad catchment covers 1404 sq km, with an average elevation of 4308 metres. It contains 272 glaciers spread over 315 sq km. The number of glacial lakes in the catchment increased from seven in 1990 to 12. Settlements, infrastructure along flood path The researchers identified Qaderna, Yurod, Anyar, Rinaie and Metwan among the settlements located around 50-55 km downstream of the glacier complex. These settlements lie in the downstream Marwah valley region, with settlements and agricultural activity also extending farther along the Marusudar River in Kishtwar district. The study noted that new settlements and agricultural activity have emerged along riverbanks over the past two decades, increasing the number of people and assets exposed to potential flooding. The Bursar and Pakal Dul hydropower projects, situated around 90 kilometres downstream, were also considered in the broader assessment of infrastructure exposure. However, their location beyond the 85-km flood-routing domain means the study does not establish whether floodwaters would reach either facility. The researchers also warned that a future GLOF could trigger cascading hazards, including debris flows and temporary river blockages. Large volumes of loose sediment deposited along the valley could be remobilised by floodwaters, amplifying the impact farther downstream. They recommended stronger monitoring, comprehensive hazard inventories and preparedness measures across the remote catchment. "An early warning system closer to the source could provide valuable lead time during a potential outburst," the researchers said. They also called for community-level preparedness and urged authorities to factor GLOF risks into infrastructure development and land-use planning. The study, titled Unreported mass movement cascades and future Glacial Lake Outburst Flood (GLOF) hazard in Jammu and Kashmir, Western Himalaya, was authored by Ashim Sattar and Abhinav Alangadan of the Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Bhubaneswar; Shashi Kant Rai and Sunil Dhar of the Central University of Jammu; Adam Emmer of Charles University, Prague, and the University of Graz, Austria; Umesh Haritashya of the University of Dayton, US; and M. Farooq Azam of IIT Indore.

The researchers attributed the expansion to glacier retreat, meltwater inflow and repeated ice-calving events.

A reconstruction of the glacier bed placed the lake's potential maximum volume at 7.7 million cubic metres, while a separate volume-area scaling method produced a comparable estimate of 7.4 million cubic metres.
The wider Fariabaad catchment covers 1404 sq km, with an average elevation of 4308 metres.
It contains 272 glaciers spread over 315 sq km.
The number of glacial lakes in the catchment increased from seven in 1990 to 12.
Settlements, infrastructure along flood path.
These settlements lie in the downstream Marwah valley region, with settlements and agricultural activity also extending farther along the Marusudar River in Kishtwar district.
The study noted that new settlements and agricultural activity have emerged along riverbanks over the past two decades, increasing the number of people and assets exposed to potential flooding.
The Bursar and Pakal Dul hydropower projects, situated around 90 kilometres downstream, were also considered in the broader assessment of infrastructure exposure.
However, their location beyond the 85-km flood-routing domain means the study does not establish whether floodwaters would reach either facility.
The researchers also warned that a future GLOF could trigger cascading hazards, including debris flows and temporary river blockages.
Large volumes of loose sediment deposited along the valley could be remobilised by floodwaters, amplifying the impact farther downstream.
They recommended stronger monitoring, comprehensive hazard inventories and preparedness measures across the remote catchment.
"An early warning system closer to the source could provide valuable lead time during a potential outburst," the researchers said.
They also called for community-level preparedness and urged authorities to factor GLOF risks into infrastructure development and land-use planning.

The study, titled Unreported mass movement cascades and future Glacial Lake Outburst Flood (GLOF) hazard in Jammu and Kashmir, Western Himalaya, was authored by Ashim Sattar and Abhinav Alangadan of the Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Bhubaneswar; Shashi Kant Rai and Sunil Dhar of the Central University of Jammu; Adam Emmer of Charles University, Prague, and the University of Graz, Austria; Umesh Haritashya of the University of Dayton, US; and M. Farooq Azam of IIT Indore.

stories.headline: Tamil Nadu runs Supreme Court contempt risk: Lamp lit, but not at pillar on Madurai hill
stories.title: Tamil Nadu runs Supreme Court contempt risk: Lamp lit, but not at pillar on Madurai hill
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
article_sentences: Hours after it assured the Madras High Court that it would comply with the Supreme Court order, the Tamil Nadu government on Tuesday left the deepathoon, the contested stone pillar atop Thirupparankundram hill in Madurai, unlit on the Karthigai Deepam festival.
On November 20, the top court, in an interim order, had permitted lighting of the ceremonial lamp at the stone pillar on the hilltop as a one-time arrangement.
By 6 pm, the festival flame burned at its customary place near the Uchi Pillaiyar temple at the foothill, not on the pillar atop the hill.
Caught between the court and allies who keep him in office, Chief Minister C Joseph Vijay chose his allies, and the risk of contempt.
Earlier in the day, the Madurai bench of the Madras High Court held an urgent hearing to ensure compliance of the Supreme Court order.

District Collector Nishant Krishna, who was appointed by the SC as the nodal officer to ensure lighting of the deepathoon, made a personal appearance and assured that the SC order will be given effect.
“We deem it necessary to remind the District Collector that he is a public servant who is answerable only to the Hon’ble Supreme Court of India in this case.
He shall ignore any contra advice given by any other authority.
We are sure that no law officer worth his salt will counsel him to act in contravention of the order…” the High Court noted in its order.

The High Court also recorded senior advocate Gopal Sankaranarayanan’s submission that he was “on instructions from the state officials” to clarify “that the order of the Hon’ble Supreme Court would be complied with,” and that there was no need for the HC to entertain these writ petitions.
For Vijay, whose TVK fell short of a majority in its first Assembly election, the question was how much political risk he could afford for a ceremony the court had authorised for one evening.
The IUML, the VCK, the CPI, the CPI(M) and the Congress had taken a firm stand against lighting a second lamp at the contested site.

stories.headline: Amit Shah: Kartarpur corridor to open after review
stories.title: Amit Shah: Kartarpur corridor to open after review
stories.summary: Union home minister Amit Shah expressed that the Kartarpur Sahib Corridor will only reopen after addressing prevailing security issues. This corridor, which offers hassle-free access for pilgrims, was shut down following security alerts linked to Operation Sindoor. Shah highlighted the need to keep national security discussions free from political influences, while also pointing out that the corridor's placement in Pakistan stemmed from Congress party oversights during partition.

stories.headline: NSA Ajit Doval, Maldives defence minister discuss security ties at Colombo meet
stories.title: NSA Ajit Doval, Maldives defence minister discuss security ties at Colombo meet
stories.summary: National Security Advisor Ajit Doval and Maldives defense minister Hassan Rasheed discussed security cooperation at the Colombo Security Conclave. This meeting marked the first high-level interaction between the two countries since President Mohamed Muizzu's recent visit to Pakistan. During that visit, Maldives signed 20 agreements with Pakistan related to defense and maritime issues. Additionally, Muizzu called for resuming the Saarc summit process to enhance regional cooperation.
